name: A1 — Beginner
description: First steps in Spanish: alphabet, greetings, ser vs estar, numbers, gendered nouns, and present-tense verbs.

topics.title: Alphabet & Sounds
topics.description: The Spanish alphabet, ñ, accents, and tricky sounds

guide.intro: Spanish uses the Latin alphabet plus one extra letter — ñ — and a small set of accent marks. The good news: Spanish spelling is highly phonetic, so once you know the rules, you can read almost any word out loud.

sections.text: Spanish has the 26 English letters plus ñ (eñe). The letters CH and LL used to count as separate letters but are now treated as digraphs.
Spanish vowels each have exactly one sound, no matter the word. Unlike English where 'a' can sound like in 'cat', 'father', or 'about', Spanish 'a' is always 'ah'.
ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon'. It's a completely separate letter — año (year) and ano (anus) are different words, so the tilde matters!
Single 'r' between vowels is a soft flap (like the 't' in American 'butter'). Double 'rr' or 'r' at the start of a word is a strong trill — practice by purring like a cat.
Spanish 'j' is like a strong English 'h' (from the back of the throat). Spanish 'g' before e or i sounds the same — so 'gente' and 'jefe' both start with that throaty sound.
LL is pronounced like English 'y' in most regions (in Argentina it sounds like 'sh'). Y by itself is also 'ee' and means 'and'.
The accent does two things: it shows which syllable to stress, and it distinguishes word pairs that are otherwise spelled identically.
Spanish opens questions with an upside-down ¿ and exclamations with ¡. They tell the reader the tone from the very first word, since Spanish word order doesn't always change in questions.
On a US keyboard, get ¿ with Option+Shift+? and ¡ with Option+1 (Mac), or use Alt codes / character shortcuts on Windows.

lessons.title: Vowels: only 5 sounds
lessons.description: Master the 5 Spanish vowels — each has one pure sound

exercises.prompt: How many vowels does Spanish have?
exercises.explanation: Spanish has five vowels: a, e, i, o, u — each with a single, consistent sound.
Spanish 'a' is always the open 'ah' sound — never like English 'cat' or 'cake'.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like English 'ee' in 'see'?
exercises.explanation: Spanish 'i' is always 'ee'. So 'sí' (yes) sounds exactly like English 'see'.
Spanish 'u' is always the 'oo' sound, like English 'food' or 'boot'.

exercises.prompt: Spanish 'e' sounds like the 'e' in English ___.
exercises.explanation: Spanish 'e' is the short 'eh' sound, like in 'bet' or 'get'.

exercises.prompt: Match the vowel to its sound

exercises.explanation: c-A-s-A — two 'ah' sounds. Every Spanish vowel you see, you pronounce.

exercises.prompt: Unlike English, Spanish vowels never become ___ (unstressed schwa).
exercises.explanation: English unstressed vowels often become 'uh' (about → uh-bout). Spanish vowels stay pure.

exercises.prompt: Which word has THREE different vowel sounds?
exercises.explanation: a-i-r-e: three different vowels (a, i, e). 'casa' and 'mesa' have only 2 distinct vowels.

lessons.description: The two sounds Spanish has that English doesn't

exercises.explanation: ñ = palatal 'ny'. 'español' sounds like 'es-pa-NYOL'.

exercises.explanation: A single 'r' between vowels = quick tongue tap. 'pero' sounds almost like 'PE-ttoh'.

exercises.prompt: How is 'rr' (or 'r' at the start of a word) pronounced?
exercises.explanation: 'rr' is the full rolled trill — multiple flutters of the tongue. 'perro' has a rolled rr; 'pero' (but) has a soft flap.
One r vs two — and you'd better roll those two! 'perro' = dog; 'pero' = but.

options: like English 'h' but stronger, from the throat

exercises.prompt: How does 'g' sound before 'e' or 'i' (as in 'gente')?
exercises.explanation: Before e/i, Spanish 'g' becomes throaty — same sound as 'j'. So 'gente' and a hypothetical 'jente' would sound the same.

exercises.explanation: 'll' usually sounds like English 'y'. 'llamar' = 'ya-MAR'. (In Argentina/Uruguay it sounds like 'sh' — 'sha-MAR'.)

exercises.explanation: 'g' is hard before a, o, u (gato, gota, gusto) and throaty before e, i (gente, gigante).
H is silent — sounds like 'OH-la'.

exercises.prompt: What does the accent mark (´) do?
exercises.explanation: The accent points to the stressed syllable AND distinguishes word pairs like tu/tú, si/sí.
tú = you (subject). tu (no accent) = your.
tu casa = your house. tú = you.
sí = yes; si = if. Same letters, totally different meaning.
él = he (subject pronoun). el = the (masculine article).

exercises.explanation: Two accents: él (he, not 'the') and está (is, not 'this').
más = more (common). mas (no accent) = but, very literary.
'más' takes the accent — it means 'more'.

topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Hello, goodbye, please, thank you — and the tú/usted distinction

guide.intro: Spanish greetings are warm and varied — and they have different forms depending on time of day and how formal you want to sound.

sections.text: Note 'buenos' (días) is masculine plural, but 'buenas' (tardes/noches) is feminine plural. That's because día is masculine even though it ends in -a!

Spanish has two words for 'you' in the singular. Tú is informal — for friends, family, kids, peers. Usted is formal — for strangers, older people, customers, professional contexts. Usted takes the same verb endings as 'he/she' (él/ella).
In Spain, tú is used very widely — even with strangers in casual settings. In much of Latin America, usted is more common with anyone you don't know well. When in doubt, start with usted.

exercises.explanation: Used until about noon.
Used from noon until early evening.
Used as both a greeting and farewell in the evening/night.

exercises.explanation: Spanish adjectives agree with their noun's gender. 'día' is a famous exception — ends in -a but is masculine.

topics.title: Subject Pronouns
topics.description: Yo, tú, él, ella — and why Spanish often drops them

guide.intro: Spanish has subject pronouns just like English — but it also has a superpower: it can drop them entirely. Because each verb form already shows who's doing the action, you usually don't need 'yo' or 'tú' at all.

rows: only used in Spain; Latin America uses ustedes
formal in Spain; standard 'you all' in Latin America

sections.text: Spanish verb endings tell you the subject. 'Hablo español' literally means 'speak Spanish' — but the -o ending of 'hablo' already means 'I', so you don't need to say 'yo'. Native speakers usually drop the pronoun unless they want to emphasize the subject or clear up ambiguity.
Use the pronoun for contrast: 'Yo hablo español, él habla inglés' (I speak Spanish; HE speaks English). Otherwise, dropping is the natural choice.
Group pronouns have gender. Use -os for a group of all men or a mixed group. Use -as only when EVERY person in the group is female.
For 'you all', Spain uses 'vosotros/vosotras' for friends and 'ustedes' for formal. Latin America has dropped 'vosotros' completely — 'ustedes' covers both informal and formal you-all.
If you're learning Latin American Spanish, focus on ustedes for all plural 'you'. Vosotros is rarely used outside Spain.

exercises.explanation: With accent: él = he. Without: el = the.
Spanish doesn't capitalize 'yo' the way English capitalizes 'I' — only at the start of a sentence.
Same letters, different words: él (he) vs el (the masculine article).
Vosotros (you all, informal) is essentially Spain-only. Latin America uses 'ustedes' for both formal and informal you-all.

exercises.prompt: In Mexico, 'you all' (a group of friends) is:
exercises.explanation: In Latin America, 'ustedes' covers both formal and informal you-all.
Mixed gender groups use the masculine form, even if mostly female. (Yes, it's a grammar rule with criticism.)

topics.title: Ser vs Estar
topics.description: Two verbs for 'to be' — the heart of Spanish

guide.intro: English has ONE verb for 'to be'. Spanish has TWO: ser and estar. They are not interchangeable. Picking the wrong one can change the meaning of a sentence — sometimes drastically. Get this right and the rest of A1 falls into place.

sections.text: SER describes what something IS — identity, origin, profession, time, permanent traits. ESTAR describes how something IS RIGHT NOW — location, state, feeling, condition.

rows: Location (Estoy en casa — I'm at home)
Origin (Soy de Perú — I'm from Peru)
Temporary state (El café está caliente — The coffee is hot)
Time/date (Son las dos — It's two o'clock)

sections.text: Tricky pairs — same English, different Spanish
Location uses ESTAR — even when the location is permanent! 'Madrid está en España' (Madrid is in Spain). The one exception: events use SER: 'La fiesta es en mi casa' (The party is at my house).
SER → DOCTOR: Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship. ESTAR → PLACE: Position, Location, Action (ongoing), Condition, Emotion.

exercises.explanation: Name = identity = ser.
Origin = ser. Always.
Profession = ser. (Spanish doesn't even use 'un' here — Es profesor, NOT Es un profesor.)
Permanent trait = ser.
Origin always takes ser. 'Soy de México' = I'm from Mexico.

exercises.prompt: 'Time identifier: It is two o'clock' → ___ las dos.
exercises.explanation: Time uses ser. Plural because two o'clock (las dos).

exercises.explanation: Days of the week = ser (identity/time).

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Count from 1 to 100, ask prices, give your age

guide.intro: Spanish numbers follow mostly regular patterns — once you know 1–15 and the tens, you can build everything up to 99.

sections.text: 16–29 fuse the ten + 'y' + digit into one word with a slight sound change: diez y seis → dieciséis.
From 30 onward, you write three words: ten + y (and) + digit. 'treinta y uno' = 31.
'uno' becomes 'un' before a masculine noun and 'una' before a feminine noun: un libro (one book), una mesa (one table), veintiún años (21 years — with accent!).
In Spanish, you HAVE years, you don't BE years. 'I am 25 years old' → 'Tengo 25 años' (I have 25 years). NEVER 'Soy 25.'

exercises.explanation: 'uno' is the counting form. Before nouns it becomes 'un' (masc) or 'una' (fem).
diez + y + seis fused = dieciséis. Notice the accent.
dieciséis, diecisiete… are single words (not 'diez y seis').
21 is written as one fused word: veintiuno.
From 31 on, write 3 words: ten + y + digit.

guide.intro: Spanish verbs end in -ar, -er, or -ir. Each group has a regular set of present-tense endings. Learn the patterns, then you can conjugate hundreds of verbs.

sections.text: Notice that -ER and -IR endings only differ in the nosotros (-emos vs -imos) and vosotros (-éis vs -ís) forms. The other four forms are identical.

TENER is used for many things English uses 'to be' for: age (tengo 25 años), hunger (tengo hambre), thirst (tengo sed), cold (tengo frío), heat (tengo calor), fear (tengo miedo). Memorize 'tengo + X' patterns!

topics.title: Articles & Gender
topics.description: El, la, los, las — every noun has a gender

guide.intro: Every Spanish noun is either MASCULINE or FEMININE — even objects, ideas, and abstract things. The article and any adjectives must match the noun's gender. This is the second biggest source of English-speaker errors (after ser/estar).

sections.text: In general, nouns ending in -O are masculine and nouns ending in -A are feminine. But there are important exceptions you should learn early.

rows: el libro, el perro, el carro
la mesa, la casa, la chica
el problema, el tema, el programa
el día (day), el mapa (map), el agua*

sections.text: 'agua' is feminine but uses 'el' in the singular (el agua) because Spanish avoids 'la a-' sound clash. Plural goes back to feminine: las aguas. Adjectives stay feminine: el agua fría.
Adjectives must match. 'A red car' = un carro rojo (masc) but 'a red house' = una casa roja (fem). Possessives mostly don't care (mi libro, mi mesa), but nuestro/nuestra and adjectives do.
Learn the article WITH the noun. Don't memorize 'libro' — memorize 'el libro'. This saves you from gender mistakes later.

guide.intro: Question words in Spanish are surprisingly close to English question words. The biggest news: question words ALWAYS take an accent, even when they look the same as a non-question version of the word.

sections.text: All question words carry a written accent. 'que' (without accent) = 'that, which'; 'qué' (with accent) = 'what?'. Same letters, different meaning.
English uses 'do/does' to form questions ('Do you live here?'). Spanish doesn't. Just put the verb after the question word — or just raise intonation for yes/no questions.
¿Por qué? (two words, with accent) = 'why?'. Porque (one word, no accent) = 'because'. Question vs answer.
'¿Qué…?' usually asks for a definition or identification ('What is X?'). '¿Cuál…?' asks 'which one?' from a known set.

guide.intro: Colors are great vocabulary AND great practice for the two big adjective rules: agreement (gender and number) and position (usually after the noun).

sections.text: 1) Agreement: Adjectives must match the noun in gender and number. 2) Position: Spanish adjectives normally come AFTER the noun, not before.

guide.intro: Spanish describes weather in three patterns: 'hace' + noun (it makes...), 'está' + adjective (it is...), and individual verbs (llueve, nieva). And remember: people don't BE cold — people HAVE cold.

sections.text: For most weather, use the impersonal 'hace' (from hacer = to make) plus a noun. Literally 'it makes sun', 'it makes cold'.
For people, use TENER, not estar. 'I'm cold' = 'Tengo frío' (I have cold). 'I'm hot' = 'Tengo calor'. Never 'soy frío' or 'estoy caliente'! ('Estoy caliente' has a sexual meaning — be careful.)
